title: Pictograph Reader
context: Grade 4, the heart of the chapter. An adult sees pictures being counted. What is actually being learnt is that a picture stands for a number only through the key, and that a question about one row is answered from that row alone. The book's own answer key gets exactly that wrong once: for the monuments row of the exercise, three heads at three students each, it prints the total of every row on the pictograph. The kites pictograph in the same section draws every kite yellow whatever its row; this tool draws each row in its own colour.

writeup.why: Read what one symbol stands for from the key, turn each row into a number, compare the rows, and answer a question from the row it asks about.
writeup.look: A pictograph board with a title strip, a key card that starts face down, a compare rail beside it and a row lamp.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Pictograph Reader' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the symbols counted in the row being read, one number in ink, and beside it the rows read against the rows on the board. The first climbs by one as each symbol is counted, shows a half for a half symbol, and starts again when a new row is tapped. The rows read climb by one as each row's number lands. The number a row stands for is never written here, and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The pictograph board fills the left of the working area, 840 by 440 at 64,212. Its title strip runs along its top, 840 by 44, and says what the data is about in near-black type. Below it stand up to six rows, each 56 tall with 8 between, from 268 to 644. Each row has its name in a cell 150 wide at the left, then its symbols from 226, each 48 wide with 10 between, up to ten. A row holds at most one half symbol, the left half of the whole, and it comes last. The row's number is written with its unit in a tag 90 wide just beyond the row's last symbol. When the rows name colours, each row's symbols are that row's colour and the key's symbol is plain grey; otherwise every symbol is green. The key card stands at the top right, 220 by 150 at 924,212, and starts face down. Until it is turned, a tapped row counts its symbols into the running count and its tag stays an empty outlined box. Turned, it shows one whole symbol, and half a symbol where the board uses one, each with what it stands for. The row reader then takes the key's value once under each symbol of a tapped row in amber, and half of it under a half symbol. The row's number then lands in its tag. The compare rail stands under the key card, 220 by 290 at 924,376. It has up to six places, one above another from the largest number at the top, each 40 tall with 10 between. Two equal numbers share one place, side by side under one near-black bracket. The row lamp sits in the name column: a tap on a row's name lays the pale sky blue band behind that row alone and dims every other row. The all-rows control stands at the lower right, 200 by 56 at 924,672. It adds every row and writes the sum in reddish purple in the strip under the board, 840 by 56 at 64,668, labelled as the total for all the rows. That strip is the one place a sum of rows is written, and it never touches a single row. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, with a key for a half beside them. A word pad carries the board's own row names, so a row is answered by its name, and the words most, least, same and total. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A question about one row is answered from that row's tag, and never from the all-rows strip. The strip answers a question only when the question asks for every row together.
writeup.finish: The card shows the pictograph the child read with every row's number written, the rows in order on the compare rail, and the one row the last question asked about still lit.

phases.win: the key card turns and every row can now take a number, with the title telling what it counts
phases.does: tries to give the lit row a number, then turns the key card and reads the title
phases.goal: the key says what one symbol stands for, and the title says what the data is about
phases.says: How many does this row stand for? What do you need to know first?
phases.check: A row has four pictures and no key. Can you say how many things it shows?
phases.feels: the pictures are only pictures until the key card turns, and then every row can become a number
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, pin a pictograph of books read by four groups on the wall, with its key covered by a sticky note. Ask how many books one group read, and let the class find that nobody can say. Lift the note. Then read the title and ask what the chart is about. The chapter defines the key in one passing sentence and names the title only in a label beside its kites. So say both aloud: the key says what one symbol stands for, and the title says what the data is about.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does the key card say? Second rung, the phase's: what is this pictograph about? Third rung: the board is cut to one row of two symbols with the key turned, and the child reads that one row. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the symbols are there to be counted, and a count feels like an answer.
wrong.move: gives the number of symbols as the answer, three apples, while the key card is still face down.
wrong.screen: the running count holds the three symbols, and the row's tag stays an empty outlined box. The key card gives one slow pulse. Once it is turned, the row reader takes its value under each symbol and the tag fills. The child's three stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the key card is the only place a number is printed, and it sits beside every row alike.
wrong.move: reads the key's number as every row's number, so a key of ten makes every row ten.
wrong.screen: the row reader takes the ten under the first symbol only, and the tag reads ten. It then carries on under each symbol in turn, and the tag climbs to thirty for a row of three. The child's ten stays beside it.

wrong.why: the row names are groups, and a group sounds like a number of children.
wrong.move: reads a chart of books read by four groups as a count of children, because the rows are groups of children.
wrong.screen: the title strip lights, and its words are set beside the child's answer. Each row's tag writes its unit, books, after its number, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a pictograph with its title strip showing and its key card face down, and one row lit
phases.soWhat: The key says what one symbol stands for, and the title says what the data is about.
phases.concept: The key says what one symbol stands for

phases.win: the key's value is added once under each symbol and the row's number lands at the end of the row
phases.does: counts the symbols in the row, then takes the key once for each symbol
phases.goal: a row is its symbols counted and the key taken that many times
phases.says: Count the symbols. Then use the key for each one.
phases.check: One picture stands for five cars. How many cars do eight pictures show?
phases.feels: the same amount under every symbol, climbing along the row to the number at its end
phases.hands: Give each pair a row of paper symbols, a key card and a heap of counters. Under each symbol they lay the key's worth of counters, then count the counters. After two or three rows, ask whether the counters were needed, and write the row as its symbols times the key.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many symbols are in the row? Second rung, the phase's: what does each one stand for? Third rung: the row is cut to two symbols, and the child writes the key under each and adds. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: there are two numbers to use, and adding is the first way the hand knows to join two numbers.
wrong.move: adds the key to the count, giving thirteen for seven umbrellas at six each.
wrong.screen: the row reader takes six under the first symbol, then six more under the second, and on down the row, the running sum written under each symbol in amber. It reaches forty-two at the seventh symbol. The child's thirteen stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the key card's symbol is the same picture, drawn at the same size, near the row.
wrong.move: counts the key card's own symbol as one of the row's, so seven symbols are read as eight.
wrong.screen: the row reader rings each of the row's symbols as it counts and stops at the row's last one. The key card's symbol is never ringed. The running count holds seven, and the tag fills with forty-two beside the child's forty-eight.

phases.screen: the pictograph with its key card turned and one row lit, its number box empty
phases.soWhat: Count the symbols in the row, then take the key that many times.

phases.win: the rows line up in order on the rail and the two equal rows stand level
phases.does: stands the rows on the compare rail and names the most, the least and the two that are the same
phases.goal: with one key for every row, the rows are compared by their numbers or by their symbols
phases.says: Which row is the longest? Which is the shortest? Are two the same?
phases.check: Rows of five, eight and five symbols share one key. Which two rows are the same?
phases.feels: with one key for every row and one size for every symbol, a longer row is a bigger number, and the rail puts them in order
phases.hands: Read a pictograph with the class for the most, the least and the two rows that are the same. The chapter's kites pictograph draws every kite yellow, even in the rows for red, blue, green and purple kites, so read it by its row names. Its worked line comparing red with green is garbled; ask how many fewer red kites were sold than green, which is four. Then show two charts side by side with different keys, and ask whether the longer row must stand for more.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which row has the most symbols? Second rung, the phase's: do all the rows use the same key? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows, and the child places both on the rail. The number keys and the row names stay open.

wrong.why: the longest row was found by its symbols, and the count of them came along with it.
wrong.move: gives nine as the most visitors, the number of symbols, instead of ninety.
wrong.screen: the rows stand on the rail by their numbers, ninety at the top. The running count shows that row's nine symbols, and its tag shows ninety. The child's nine stays in the slot.

wrong.why: on a well drawn chart the longest row is the most, and this row is the longest.
wrong.move: calls the row that reaches furthest the most, on a chart drawn by hand with the pictures of one row drawn larger.
wrong.screen: the card's rows are redrawn on the board at one size from the same edge, and the row of five large pictures comes out shorter than the row of seven. The rail puts the seven row's number above the five row's. The card stays beside the board.

wrong.why: on one chart more symbols has always meant more, and here the two rows sit side by side.
wrong.move: compares rows from two charts with different keys by their symbols, calling six symbols more than four.
wrong.screen: each row is read with its own key, six fives and four tens. Thirty and forty take their places on the rail, forty above. The two key cards stand beside their rows.

phases.screen: every row read and numbered, with the compare rail empty beside the board
phases.soWhat: With one key for every row, compare by numbers or by symbols. With different keys, compare only the numbers.

phases.win: the answer lands beside the one lit row, and the all-rows sum sits apart under the board as the total
phases.does: lights the row the question names, reads it, and sees what the all-rows control gives instead
phases.goal: a question about one row is answered from that row, and every row added gives the total for all of them
phases.says: Which row does the question ask about? Read that one.
phases.check: Four rows stand for twelve, eighteen, fifteen and nine. How many does the third row show?
phases.feels: one row lit and the rest dimmed, and the sum of every row kept in its own place under the board
phases.hands: Ask questions from a wall pictograph, some about one row and some about every row, and sort the question cards into two piles. That is the question the book's own answer key gets wrong once. The exercise asks how many students visited the monuments, a row of three heads at three students each, which is nine students, and the key prints the total of every row. Mark nine right, and have the class say what the key's number counts. Add every row when a question asks for all of them together, and say what the sum counts. It counts each thing once only when each thing sits in one row.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which row does the question name? Second rung, the phase's: does it ask about one row, or about all of them? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows, one lit, and the child reads the lit one. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: adding every row has been right for how many in all, and this question has a how many in it too.
wrong.move: adds every row and gives one hundred and five when the question asks how many chose chess.
wrong.screen: the row lamp lights the chess row alone and dims the rest. Its three faces are counted and read with the key, and fifteen lands in its tag. The all-rows sum, one hundred and five, sits apart in the strip under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the rows are close together, and the eye settles on the row it last looked at.
wrong.move: reads the row next to the one the question names.
wrong.screen: the row lamp lights the named row. The row the child read is outlined, and its name is set beside the name on the question card. The lit row is then read, and its number lands in its tag.

wrong.why: reading only the row asked has just been learnt, and a club's name sits on the card.
wrong.move: gives one club's number when the question asks how many children are in the four clubs together.
wrong.screen: the question card's word together is underlined. The all-rows control adds every row, twelve, eighteen, fifteen and nine, and fifty-four lands in the strip, labelled as the total for all the rows. Each child here is in one club, so the sum counts each child once.

phases.screen: the whole pictograph, a question card naming one row, the row lamp and the all-rows control
phases.soWhat: Read only the row a question asks about. Add every row only when it asks for all of them.

writeup.delight: The second phase, once a row's number has landed. Any symbol in that row can then be tapped. It opens like a paper packet to show what it stands for inside, the key's worth of small amber counters, then folds shut again. A half symbol opens to show half as many. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the pictograph board stands with its title strip showing, its key card face down, and one row lit. On the second the key card is turned, and one row is lit with its tag an empty outlined box. On the third every row is read and numbered, and the compare rail stands empty beside the board. On the fourth the whole pictograph stands with every tag empty, a question card naming one row sits in the slot, and the all-rows control waits under the rail. The running count at the top left holds the symbols counted in the row being read, with the rows read beside it. The answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the face-down key card, or the lit row, or the largest number, or the row the question names, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what one picture stands for. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any pictograph of up to six rows and any key, with the key card, the compare rail, the row lamp and the all-rows control all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on what the key and the title say, a row as its symbols times the key, the most, the least and the same, and reading only the row a question asks about.

Free play. Any pictograph and any key, with the lamp and the rail open.
Count the symbols again, and take the key once for each one.
Every row read with its key, the rows compared, and only the row asked read.

observations.why: A symbol stands for a number only through the key.
observations.soWhat: Read the key first, because the same pictures stand for different numbers under different keys.
observations.observe: With the key face down, the row could be counted in symbols, and its tag stayed empty.

observations.why: Every symbol in the row stands for the same amount.
observations.soWhat: A row is its symbols counted and the key taken that many times.
observations.observe: The key's value was written once under each symbol, and the row's number was the last of them.

observations.why: With one key for every row, the same symbols make the same number.
observations.soWhat: When every row uses the same key, the rows can be compared by their symbols as well as by their numbers.
observations.observe: Two rows with the same number of symbols shared one place on the rail.

observations.why: The question named one row, and the sum of every row answers a different question.
observations.soWhat: Read only the row a question asks about, and add every row when the question asks for all of them.
observations.observe: The lit row's number landed in its tag, and the sum of every row sat apart under the board.

serves.exercise: reading the pictograph of outdoor visits for the most and least popular, the two liked equally, and the students who visited the monuments

source_tool.description: A pictograph board fills the stage: a title strip across its top, a name at the start of every row, rows of one symbol drawn at one size, and a key card beside it that starts face down. Until the key card is turned, a tapped row can only be counted in symbols, and its number stays an empty box. Once it is turned, the key card shows one whole symbol and what it stands for, and a row reader takes that value once for each symbol and writes the row's number, with its unit, at the end of the row. When the rows name colours, every symbol in a row is drawn in that row's colour. A compare rail stands the rows' numbers side by side from the largest to the smallest, so the most and the least sit at its ends and equal rows stand level. A question card sits in the slot, and a row lamp lights only the row the question names, dimming the rest. An all-rows control adds every row and writes the sum under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, never beside a single row.
source_tool.art_direction: A wall chart with a hidden key / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the symbols again, and take the key once for each one.
voice.onNext: Another question. Which row does it ask about?
voice.opening: A pictograph, and its key card face down. What does one picture stand for?
voice.onFinish: Every row read with its key, the rows compared, and only the row asked read.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any pictograph and any key, with the lamp and the rail open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The key says what one symbol stands for

placement.where: After a pictograph on chart paper, with a title and a key, has been read by the class from question cards, and before the printed pictographs are read. The tool is what keeps the key face down until it is read, so a row cannot become a number without it, and what lights only the row a question names, which a printed page leaves to the reader.

answer_key.rule: A pictograph shows data with symbols. The key says what one symbol stands for, and the title says what the data is about. A row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times. When every row uses the same key, the rows can be compared by their symbols: the row with the most symbols stands for the most. A question about one row is answered from that row only. Adding every row gives the total for all the rows, which answers a different question.
answer_key.wrong: The row reader counts the row again symbol by symbol, then takes the key once for each symbol with the running sum said aloud, and the row lamp relights the one row the question names. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The two rows look the same: 3 pictures each.
The keys are different, so the pictures stand for different numbers.
First row: 3 x 2 = 6 apples. Second row: 3 x 10 = 30 apples.
items.answer: 6 apples in the first row and 30 in the second
items.question: Two pictographs each show a row of 3 apple pictures. The first key says one apple picture stands for 2 apples. The second says one apple picture stands for 10 apples. How many apples does each row show?
items.checkpoint: The key says what one symbol stands for, so the same pictures can stand for different numbers.
items.misconception: Reading both rows as 3 apples because the pictures look the same, without reading either key.

steps: Count the symbols in the June row: there are 7.
The key says each symbol stands for 6 umbrellas.
items.question: In a pictograph of umbrellas sold, one umbrella picture stands for 6 umbrellas. The row for June holds 7 umbrella pictures. How many umbrellas were sold in June?
items.checkpoint: Count the symbols in the row, then multiply by the key.
items.misconception: Adding the key to the count, 7 + 6 = 13, instead of taking 6 seven times.

steps: Every row uses the same key, so the row with the most symbols shows the most: Tuesday, 9 x 10 = 90.
The row with the fewest symbols shows the fewest: Wednesday, 4 x 10 = 40.
Monday and Thursday both hold 6 symbols, so both show 6 x 10 = 60.
items.answer: Tuesday the most, 90; Wednesday the fewest, 40; Monday and Thursday the same, 60 each
items.question: A pictograph of visitors to a book fair has the key one person picture for 10 visitors. Monday holds 6 pictures, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 4 and Thursday 6. Which day had the most visitors, which the fewest, and which two days had the same number?
items.checkpoint: When every row uses the same key, the rows can be compared by their symbols too.
items.misconception: Giving 9 as the most visitors, the number of symbols, instead of 90 from the key.

steps: The question names one sport, so light only the chess row.
It holds 3 faces, and 3 x 5 = 15 children.
Adding every row gives 21 faces, 105 children: the total for all four sports, which answers a different question.
items.question: A pictograph shows the sport each child in a class chose, one face for 5 children: swimming 6 faces, chess 3, skating 4 and football 8. How many children chose chess?
items.checkpoint: Read only the row the question asks about.
items.misconception: Adding every row and giving 105, the total for all four sports, when the question asks about chess alone.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A pictograph has rows of fish pictures but no key. Can you tell how many fish one row shows?
items.final_answer: No. Without the key you cannot tell what one fish picture stands for

items.question: A pictograph is titled Cups of Tea Sold This Week, and its key reads one cup picture for 10 cups. What does the title tell you, and what does the key tell you?
items.final_answer: The title says what the data is about, the cups of tea sold this week. The key says one cup picture stands for 10 cups

items.question: One shell picture stands for 3 shells. A row holds 8 shell pictures. How many shells does it show?
One car picture stands for 5 cars. The rows for three car parks hold 9, 6 and 7 car pictures. How many cars are in each car park?
One leaf picture stands for 4 leaves. Groups A, B, C and D hold 5, 8, 3 and 5 leaf pictures. Which two groups collected the same number of leaves, and how many each?
items.final_answer: Groups A and D, 20 leaves each

items.question: One bowl picture stands for 8 bowls of rice served. Monday holds 3 bowl pictures, Tuesday 6, Wednesday 5 and Thursday 2. On which day were the most bowls served, and on which the fewest?
items.final_answer: Tuesday the most, 48 bowls; Thursday the fewest, 16 bowls

items.question: A pictograph of fruit sold at a stall, one fruit picture for 6 fruits, holds 5 pictures for apples, 2 for pears, 7 for plums and 4 for figs. How many pears were sold?
items.final_answer: 12 pears. Read only the pears row: 2 x 6 = 12

items.question: A pictograph of four clubs, one face for 3 children, holds 4 faces for art, 6 for music, 5 for dance and 3 for science. Each child is in one club. How many children are in the dance club, and how many are in the four clubs together?
items.final_answer: 15 in the dance club, and 54 in all, because 12 + 18 + 15 + 9 = 54

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: starts face down and turns to show one symbol and what it stands for
says what the data in the pictograph is about
counts a row's symbols and takes the key that many times
writes each row's number, with its unit, at the end of the row
stands the rows' numbers side by side from the largest to the smallest
lights only the row a question names and dims the rest

teaching_notes: Pin a pictograph of books read by four groups on the wall before the tool is opened, with a title and a key, and have pairs answer question cards from it. Ask which cards needed one row and which needed every row. That is the question the book's own answer key gets wrong once: the exercise asks how many students visited the monuments, a row of three heads at three students each, which is nine, and the key prints the total of every row. Mark nine right, and have the class say what the other number counts. Keep the count of symbols and the number apart in every answer, and say the unit. The kites pictograph in the section draws every kite yellow, even in the rows for red, blue, green and purple kites, so read it by its row names; in the tool each row is drawn in its own colour. The worked conclusion under it is printed as the number of less red kites sold than green; say how many fewer red kites were sold than green, which is four.
generation_prompt: Build a pictograph reading tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A pictograph board fills most of the working area: a title strip across its top, a name at the start of each of up to six rows, and in each row a run of one symbol drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same left edge, with at most one half symbol, the left half of the whole, at a row's end. When the row names are colours, each row's symbols are drawn in that colour; otherwise all symbols share one colour. A key card beside the board starts face down; until it is turned, tapping a row counts its symbols into the running count at the top left of the canvas but leaves the row's number box empty. Once turned, it shows one whole symbol and what it stands for, and the row reader writes each row's number, with its unit, at the row's end, taking the key once per symbol and half the key for a half symbol. A compare rail beside the board stands the rows' numbers from the largest to the smallest, equal numbers level. A row lamp lights the one row the question card names and dims the rest; an all-rows control writes the sum of every row under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Turn the key card first. Count the symbols in a row. Use the key for each symbol. Line the rows up to compare them. Read only the row the question asks about.
